heading: Review | Freedom and Despair: Israeli scholar David Shulman’s notes from the West Bank
author: Stanly Johny
paragraphs: The Israeli-occupied West Bank has been divided into Areas A, B, and C, as part of the Oslo Accords. The Palestinian Authority, based in Ramallah, has some security and civil administration powers in Area A, and civil authority in Area B, while the Israelis have full civil and military control over Area C, which covers 62% of the West Bank. Area C is home to some 3 lakh Palestinians and roughly 4.9 lakh Jewish settlers.

Modern Jewish settlements in the West Bank started soon after the 1967 war when Israel captured the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan and the Gaza Strip from Egypt. Today, some 7.5 lakh Jewish settlers live in the West Bank and East Jerusalem. Over the years, the settler community has become politically powerful — they have their own parties and ministers.

The extremist, far-right sections of the settlers want to expel the Palestinians from their villages and grab their land. Israeli politicians have repeatedly called for annexing the settlements. In recent years, settlers in the West Bank have stepped up attacks against local Palestinians, seizing their land, torching their homes, and unleashing physical attacks on them. It is these stories of terror and horror that David Shulman brings to us from the South Hebron Hills, a rural area at the southern tip of the West Bank, which is part of Area C, in his book, Freedom and Despair: Notes from the West Bank.

Shulman, an Israeli scholar of South Asian languages and religion, has never shied away from critiquing what he calls the “monstrosity” of the Israeli occupation of Palestine. When this reviewer met him in January 2025 in Chennai, he said “the army, the police, the military courts, the Israeli media, public and social media, and the government, which funds and supports the settlements, all constitute [the] system” that preserves occupation.

In Freedom and Despair, Shulman, who is also a member of Ta’ayush (co-existence in Arabic), an Israeli-Palestinian grassroots organisation, writes about the acts of resistance by Palestinians and Israelis against this machinery of occupation. Despite some micro victories, their acts do not have any meaningful impact on the larger political course. But despair — the state of having lost all hope — should not be an end in itself. Despair, he writes, should act as a catalyst for more action, driven by “hopeless hope”.

Shulman is worried about both the victim and the aggressor, though on different scales. While occupation subjugates Palestinians to endless horrors, it transforms the occupier as well. “To impair the freedom of another people is to narrow one’s own self to a rude and bitter thing,” he writes. “For an entire people to impair the freedom is to multiply self-constriction exponentially.” Israel, according him, “has become ill and narrow at heart”.

Ta’ayush, founded in 2000 during the second intifada (uprising), works to end the Israeli occupation of Palestinian lands, stop racism, and build equal partnership between Arabs and Jews. At the micro level, the organisation has achieved a great deal: fields have been restored to owners, villages saved, homes rebuilt, and innocent Palestinians protected from arrest and torture. But Shulman also acknowledges that despite grassroots activism, Israel polity has shifted further towards the right, imprisoning Palestinians in their deserts and on their hills. “There is a bitter contrast between the wide-open vistas of the desert and the utter absence of freedom to move, even breathe, that lies at the base of their experience,” he writes. “There are moments you could weep that human beings could be like this,” he adds while describing the settler violence against Palestinians.

While despair is widespread, not doing anything is clearly not the answer. Shulman says the Jews had learned to overcome their deep passivity decades ago and rediscovered how to act in the world, defend themselves, and fight back. “Now they have to overcome the fascism that comes with blind autistic power: witness the settler, their primitive malice, their adoration of brute compulsion.” He quotes German-American rabbi and activist Joachim Prinz, who had first-hand experience of Nazi Germany in the 1930s, who said, “The most urgent, the most disgraceful, the most shameful, and the most tragic problem is silence.”

Shulman embraces Gandhian satyagraha — the non-violent assertion of a moral position — as the right way of resistance against the brutal machinery of occupation. Israeli generals and policemen prefer violent Palestinian resistance, which they can use as an excuse to tighten their control and occupation. “Violence compounds the evil. And besides, the beauty of Gandhian-style protest is that it needs no further justification. It is right in itself, worth doing for itself, for the sake of truth,” he writes.

Freedom and Despair is not just an account of the suffering of the Palestinians in the West Bank; it also offers a philosophical guidance to the micro resistance that is taking shape in both Israel and Palestine. Even the smallest act can have consequential effects. “Some day, this occupation will end,” he writes, and asks for “dogged persistence” from the peace camp.

In the final pages, Shulman writes about a friend who died young. He was an adventurer and historian. “Perhaps the last words he said to his wife were: ‘Sail into the wind’.” Those words ring true, writes the Indologist. “One who has never known the sheer joy of sailing into the wind may not understand.”
